 Lunch Box Breakfast Biscuits Sold in Convenience Stores, Vending Machines and Prison Canteens Recalled Over Listeria Risk
 Published Nov 21, 2026 12:19 PM EST 
 By
 Joseph James 
 Tim Boyle | Getty Images 
 Share on Twitter 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on WhatsApp 
 Grand Strand Sandwich Company of Longs, South Carolina, is recalling four Lunch Box breakfast biscuit sandwiches because the biscuits may be contaminated with Listeria monocytogenes , according to the company's recall announcement posted by the FDA Nov. 19. The products were sold in North Carolina, South Carolina, and Virginia.
 The sandwiches went to retail convenience stores, vending machines and prison canteens between March 2 and Nov. 10. The company said no illnesses have been reported to date.
 For shoppers in Charlotte, Raleigh, Myrtle Beach, Columbia and Richmond, these are the kind of wrapped breakfast items people grab at a gas station on the way to work. They are also sold where buyers have little access to recall news, including inside correctional facilities.
 The distribution window is long. More than eight months passed between the first shipments covered by the recall and the supplier's warning, so many of the sandwiches were likely eaten or thrown out long ago. The ones that matter now are any still sitting in store coolers, vending machines, or home refrigerators.
 Four Products and the UPCs to Check
 The recall covers the Lunch Box Bacon Egg and Cheese Biscuit, 4 ounces, UPC 0 67068 21400 8; the Lunch Box Chicken Sausage Biscuit, 3.75 ounces, UPC 0 67068 21404 6; the Lunch Box Jumbo Sausage Biscuit, 4 ounces, UPC 0 67068 21407 7; and the Lunch Box Sausage Egg & Cheese Biscuit, 5 ounces, UPC 0 67068 21402 2.
 All four come in clear plastic packaging. Each product has specific Julian date codes listed in the FDA notice, ranging from a single code for the chicken sausage biscuit to 10 codes for the bacon, egg and cheese biscuit. Shoppers should compare both the UPC and the date code on the package with the FDA list.
 The company said Dot Foods, a food distributor, notified it on Nov. 11 that biscuits it had supplied might be contaminated. The notice does not name the biscuit maker, and it does not report a positive Listeria test in the finished sandwiches. It also does not say how many sandwiches were shipped or which stores, vending companies, or prison systems received them, details that would help buyers know whether they are affected.
 Consumers can return the products to the place of purchase for a full refund or throw them away. Questions can go to the company at 843-399-2999, Monday through Thursday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. and Friday from 8 a.m. to noon Eastern.
 Another Biscuit Recall, With Its Source Unclear
 The recall arrives during a separate, widening series of Listeria recalls tied to biscuits from C.H. Guenther & Son, a San Antonio company. Fresh & Ready Foods first recalled biscuit sandwiches sold in Washington and Oregon , and MedicalDaily later reported that the recall expanded to vending products in seven Southern states .
 Whether the Grand Strand biscuits came from the same baker is not known. The Grand Strand notice mentions only Dot Foods and does not refer to C.H. Guenther. Neither company nor the FDA has publicly connected the recalls, and readers should not assume a link.
 The Longs plant has drawn FDA scrutiny before. In a 2020 FDA warning letter to Grand Strand , the agency said environmental swabs at the facility had found Listeria monocytogenes , and genetic sequencing showed the same strain in swabs collected during 2017 and 2018 inspections. The FDA said that pattern pointed to "a resident pathogen or harborage site" in the facility since 2017. The current recall is attributed to a supplier notice, not to plant testing, and public records reviewed for this report do not show whether those earlier problems were resolved.
 Who Faces the Greatest Listeria Risk
 Listeria infection is rare but serious. About 1,250 people in the U.S. get it each year and about 172 die, making it the fourth leading cause of death from foodborne illness, according to the CDC's Listeria overview .
 The highest risk falls on pregnant women, newborns, adults 65 and older, and people with weakened immune systems, including those receiving cancer treatment. Healthy people usually have only short-term symptoms such as fever, headache, nausea, and diarrhea.
 Pregnancy is the greatest concern. A pregnant woman may feel only mildly ill, while the infection can lead to miscarriage, stillbirth, premature delivery, or a life-threatening infection in the newborn. Symptoms of serious infection can appear weeks after eating contaminated food, sometimes long after a wrapper has been thrown away.
 Listeria can grow at refrigerator temperatures, which is why chilled, ready-to-eat foods are a frequent source of recalls. Recalled items should be thrown away or returned rather than reheated and eaten.
 Steps for Shoppers, Store Owners and Facilities
 Anyone who has one of the four products should not eat it. Most people who eat a contaminated food do not get sick, and people who feel well do not need testing.
 People who develop fever and muscle aches after eating one, especially if they are pregnant, older or immunocompromised, should call a clinician and mention possible Listeria exposure. A stiff neck, confusion, loss of balance or a seizure needs urgent care. Listeriosis is treated with antibiotics, and a lab test is needed to confirm it.
 Convenience store owners and vending operators can pull matching items and clean shelves and coolers that held them with hot, soapy water. Correctional facilities that stock the products can remove them from canteen inventory and tell residents, since incarcerated people often cannot check recall notices themselves.
 MedicalDaily will report if the biscuit supplier is identified, if more products are added or if illnesses are reported.

 Key Questions Answered
 Which products are recalled? Four Lunch Box biscuits: Bacon Egg and Cheese, Chicken Sausage, Jumbo Sausage, and Sausage Egg & Cheese.
 Where were they sold? In convenience stores, vending machines and prison canteens in North Carolina, South Carolina and Virginia.
 How do I know if I have one? Check the UPC and Julian date code on the package against the list in the FDA notice.
 Has anyone gotten sick? No illnesses have been reported, according to the company.
 Is this tied to the C.H. Guenther biscuit recall? That has not been confirmed. The notice names only the distributor, Dot Foods.
 Who is most at risk from Listeria? Pregnant women, newborns, adults 65 and older and people with weakened immune systems.
 What should I do with the product? Do not eat it. Return it for a full refund or throw it away.
